title: Cao Cao Punishes Himself for Trampling Crops
text:
Cao Cao was the most powerful warlord of late Han China at the end of the second century, and the founder of what became the kingdom of Wei. He was known both as a brilliant general and administrator and, in later tradition, as a cunning schemer.

A story about him survives in a work called the Cao Man Zhuan, quoted by Pei Songzhi in his fifth-century commentary on the Records of the Three Kingdoms. Once, on campaign, Cao Cao ordered that no soldier should trample the growing wheat, on pain of death. Cavalrymen dismounted and led their horses carefully through the fields.

Then Cao Cao's own horse was startled and plunged into the wheat. He called the army's registrar and asked him to decide his punishment. The registrar cited the old principle that punishments are not applied to those of the highest rank. Cao Cao answered that if he made a law and broke it himself, how could he command his men. But as the commander he could not kill himself, so he drew his sword, cut off his hair and threw it on the ground as a substitute for his head.

In that era cutting one's hair was a real disgrace, and the gesture made the point to the whole army.
lesson: The rules you set for others bind you too. When you break one, take the consequence visibly, or your rules lose their force.
source: Cao Man Zhuan, quoted by Pei Songzhi in his commentary on Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), Biography of Cao Cao
caveat: The Cao Man Zhuan was a hostile source from the rival state of Wu, which told the story to show Cao Cao's craftiness.
